newsitem.title: UK: Northern Irish peace talks to reopen amidst gloom.
newsitem.headline: Northern Irish peace talks to reopen amidst gloom.

text.p: Fractious multi-party talks on ending the Northern Ireland conflict are set to reopen on Tuesday in a gloomy atmosphere after a weekend of violence in the British-ruled province.

The talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, started almost a year ago but have done little apart from underlying the depths of mistrust between majority Protestants and minority Catholics.

The opening will undoubtedly be marked by noise and protests as the Irish Republican Army's political wing Sinn Fein -- which has been banned from the talks until the guerrillas restore a ceasefire they broke last year -- tries unsuccessfully to be admitted.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said his movement -- which benefitted from an upsurge of support in Britain's May 1 election -- had a right to take part.

"I am not going up (to the talks) to demand anything other than the rights of those people who voted for us...I hope that we are allowed into the talks tomorrow, I hope that wiser counsel prevails," he told reporters.
"I hope that there there is some sense that there are historic opportunities here which must be consolidated."
The new Labour government ended a freeze on ties with Sinn Fein after its crushing election win but made clear the door would be open only as long as the IRA desisted from violence.
This could be under threat after the IRA abandoned a large home-made bomb in a Catholic area of Belfast on Saturday. Security sources said the bomb was a trap to ensnare troops and police.
On Sunday an off-duty policeman was kicked to death in the latest upwelling of communal hatred. Protestant hardliners were blamed.
Police said some 12 high velocity shots were fired overnight at a heavily fortified British security base in the heart of Irish nationalist west Belfast.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, during a visit to London last Thursday, appealed to the IRA to "lay down your guns for good" so as to win a voice for its Sinn Fein political wing in talks.
Prime Minister Tony Blair met Mitchell for 20 minutes on Monday accompanied by his deputies at the talks, Canadian general John de Chastelaine and ex-Finnish prime minister Harri Holkeri.

"Obviously, in advance of the talks restarting tomorrow, he (Blair) wanted to express the government's thanks again for what they've done already, to confirm our commitment to finding a peace settlement and to encourage them as they go about their business in the future," a government spokeswoman said.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton signalled he might re-impose a ban on meetings between officials and the Sinn Fein after the IRA bomb incident.
Contacts had been frozen since February 1996 when the Irish guerrillas set off a huge bomb in eastern London killing two civilians and devastating property.
Sinn Fein officials have held two rounds of inconclusive talks with British officials and a third is planned, but no date has yet been set.
